h1: Superdelic hops and their red berry character in hazy IPA
title: Superdelic Hops and Red Berry Hazy IPA | Craft Beer School
desc: What Superdelic hops bring to a hazy IPA: red berry, candy and tropical notes, plus the rates and timing that keep them bright.
teaser: Superdelic tastes of red berries and sweets. In a hazy IPA that is either brilliant or too much, depending on how you use it.
standfirst: Superdelic is one of the newer New Zealand hops, known for red berry and candy aromas rarely found in a hop. It shines in hazy IPA. This guide covers what it tastes like and how to keep it from turning into a fruit cordial.
sections: A New Zealand hop that tastes of berries

Superdelic is a newer release from New Zealand, sold by NZ Hops. Most hops are described with citrus, pine, tropical fruit or herbs. Superdelic is described with red berries, boiled sweets and jellybeans, which is unusual enough to get brewers' attention.

The berry note sits on top of a tropical base, with pineapple and some citrus. It is a dual purpose hop with alpha acids high enough to bitter with, though few brewers would waste it on the kettle. Its value is in the oils. Like most New Zealand varieties it carries a fairly rich oil content for its weight.

Hazy IPA is built for this kind of hop. A soft body, low perceived bitterness and a fruity yeast all give a berry and candy character room to show. In a crisp, bitter West Coast IPA the same aroma can feel out of place, like a dessert served with the main course.

A typical 20 litre hazy IPA might use a grist of 75% pale malt, 15% oats and 10% wheat, with an OG near 1.065. Bitter lightly, around 20 to 25 IBU, so the bitterness does not fight the fruit. Most of the hops go into the whirlpool and the dry hop.
Rates and timing for a bright berry note

We would start here for 20 litres:

  • Whirlpool: 50 to 70 g at around 75 °C for 20 to 30 minutes.
  • First dry hop: 40 to 60 g during active fermentation, around day two.
  • Second dry hop: 80 to 100 g after fermentation, once gravity has stopped falling.

The early dry hop is common in hazy IPA because yeast activity can transform some hop compounds and change the fruit character. The trade off is that active fermentation also carries away some aroma with the CO2. The late dry hop puts the brightest aroma back.

Keep total dry hop weight sensible. Past about 8 g per litre, the risk of hop burn rises fast. A berry hop with a harsh, grassy finish is a poor result.

Superdelic can get lost beside very loud hops. Pair it with something that supports the fruit rather than drowning it. A citrus or stone fruit hop works. A hop known for orange and vanilla, such as Lotus, can make an interesting sweet shop combination if that is the beer you want.

Avoid pairing it with hops that carry strong onion, garlic or dank notes. Those sulphur heavy characters clash badly with candy and berry. Test any new blend with a hop tea first: steep the two hops together in hot water and smell it before committing 150 g to a batch.
Keeping it fresh in Indian heat

New release hops often arrive in India in small lots and can sit with importers for a while. Ask for the crop year before you buy. A pellet from the latest harvest kept frozen will be far brighter than one that has spent a summer in a warehouse.

Hazy IPA is also the least forgiving style for the cold chain after packaging. Its fruit fades within weeks if the beer sits warm. If you are brewing Superdelic for friends or a pub tap, keep the finished beer cold, ideally at 2 to 4 °C. Drink it young.
Yeast and water shape the fruit

Hop aroma does not arrive in the glass on its own. The yeast you choose and the water you brew with shape it heavily. Hazy IPA strains, often derived from English ale yeast, produce fruity esters that blend with Superdelic's berry note. A neutral American strain shows the hop more plainly but gives less of the soft fruit salad effect.

Ferment at 18 to 20 °C. Warmer than that and esters climb fast. You may end up unable to tell which fruit came from the hop and which from the yeast. Cooler and the yeast may not finish cleanly, leaving diacetyl that turns a berry beer buttery.

Water matters too. Hazy IPA usually leans towards chloride, with a chloride to sulphate ratio around 2:1, for a rounder, softer mouthfeel. A high sulphate water makes the bitterness sharper and the berry note thinner. If your water is hard borewell water, start from RO water and add calcium chloride and a little gypsum to taste.

The hard part with Superdelic is not getting the berry note. It is keeping it. Aroma loss happens through oxidation, through yeast transforming compounds and through hop oils binding to yeast and settling out. Each one is a separate mechanism with a separate fix.

Brew one batch with a single late dry hop and one with the two stage schedule above. Taste them side by side at one week and three weeks. Which keeps its berries longer tells you which process fits your kit.
faqs: Red berries, boiled sweets and jellybeans, on a tropical base with pineapple and some citrus.
Is Superdelic good in a West Coast IPA?
It can work, but its candy and berry character suits the soft, low bitterness body of a hazy IPA better.
How much Superdelic should I use?
For a 20 litre hazy IPA, start with 50 to 70 g in the whirlpool and 120 to 160 g across two dry hops, keeping the total dry hop under about 8 g per litre.
